b: For eight years now, I’ve worked on a campus where there are a few different entities, mainly a K-12 school. It is a small/close campus. Most of the people working on campus also go to the church, so I also see them on a social basis.

This past year, there was an opening for a school counselor. I have my master’s in counseling and have been working to get my full license for the past 2.5 years, working at another job in the counseling field. I didn’t initially apply because the posting said they wanted someone with experience working at a school, which I don’t have in that capacity. However, after talking with people, including the head school counselor, I realized the other counselors on staff had not had school experience prior either, so I decided to apply. I was told immediately by HR that I would not even be granted an interview because of the lack of school experience. I reached out for feedback on what skills they thought I would be lacking without that experience. Weeks after I asked, I got a meeting with three of the higher admin. However, at that point they had already hired someone else and the meeting was just conciliatory and the feedback was a generic list of the skills they wanted for the position. It did not seem like they had even looked at my resume, as I have most of the skills on the list.

When I looked her the person they hired, it turns out she also does not have any school counseling experience. In fact, her credentials and experience look very similar to mine. So now I’m confused as to what happened and hurt that I wasn’t even given a chance, given that I have more than just a professional relationship with these people. The HR person who initially told me I wouldn’t get an interview no longer works there, but I don’t know what led to their leaving.

I’m struggling because I do have to see these people, even though I’m planning on leaving the campus when I get my license, as I will still see them at church functions. I’m wondering if it would be helpful to send them an email asking what happened and letting them know that it hurt to have given so much to the campus and not even be given a chance. And, overall, there are concerns with others on campus that the higher admin is becoming very corporate and soulless when we are a Christian organization at our core. I would also want them to know those concerns, with the goal that they would work to change that. Do I write the email? Would it make any difference?
Don’t send the email. Write it if writing it might make you feel better, but don’t send it.

I know this feels very personal. But I don’t think an email will give you the thing you want, which is some recognition that your years of work meant something, because the people involved in the hiring process don’t see it in those terms.

There are so many things that could have led to this happening — they might have already had this person in mind to hire from the beginning, or they might have had some specific concern about your candidacy that they didn’t share with you, or they might have really thought they required school experience but then changed their mind because they were wowed by some other aspect of this person’s candidacy, or she was someone’s niece, or who knows what. They’re probably not going to give you a satisfying answer (especially since they already had a chance to in that feedback meeting and declined to).

They’re also unlikely to take feedback about the wider situation on campus in a truly constructive way. There are ways to raise concerns like that about the place you’re working, but it’s not in an email that’s primarily about not getting interviewed or hired (and those other ways still have relatively low chances of success in the type of situation you described).

Regarding seeing them at church, I don’t know if this helps or makes it worse, but they probably won’t be associating you with this in their heads since that hasn’t been their focus. So while you might be feeling awkward, they likely won’t be — so if you want to just skip by the whole thing, you can! But at the same time, if you need some space right now, take it. Sit somewhere else, arrive a little later, leave a little earlier, spend time with people who make you feel comfortable. But remember that you don’t have to resolve this with your colleagues in order to move past it yourself.
